en: The *Śālistamba Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, translated during the Eastern Jin period (translator lost), appended to the Eastern Jin Records.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
There was a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus,
together with a multitude of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra went to the place where Maitreya was walking.
Maitreya and Śāriputra were both seated upon a rock.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked Maitreya:
"Today, the World-Honored One beheld a rice seedling and spoke these words."
"O bhikṣus, to see the twelve links of dependent origination is to see the Dharma."
This is precisely seeing the Buddha.
At that time, having spoken thus, the World-Honored One remained silent.
Maitreya, [this is so].
World-Honored One, for what reason did you preach this sūtra?
Furthermore, by what meaning do you say that seeing the twelve links of dependent origination is itself seeing the Dharma?
To see the Dharma is to see the Buddha.
For what reason is this said?
What is the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination?
"How is it that seeing dependent origination is seeing the Dharma?
How is it that seeing the Dharma is seeing the Buddha?
At that time, Maitreya said to Śāriputra:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has constantly taught:
"To see the twelve links of dependent origination is to see the Dharma;
to see the Dharma is to see the Buddha."
Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination:
ignorance conditions volitional formations;
volitional formations condition consciousness.
Consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases;
the six sense bases condition contact.
Contact conditions feeling;
feeling conditions craving;
craving conditions clinging.
With grasping as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair arise.
The accumulation of all sufferings serves as the cause for the great mass of suffering;
therefore, the Buddha taught the twelve links of dependent origination.
How is it that this dharma constitutes a factor of the right path and the fruit of nirvāṇa?
The Tathāgata has briefly explained this Dharma.
What is a Buddha? It is one who is able to awaken to all dharmas.
Therefore, he is named Buddha.
If one perceives the true Dharma-body with the eye of wisdom,
one can accomplish the dharmas studied for Bodhi.
How is it that seeing the twelve links of dependent origination is itself seeing the Dharma?
Seeing the Dharma is itself seeing the Buddha.
Thus has the Buddha spoken.
The twelve links of dependent origination arise in constant succession; seeing them as non-arising according to reality is non-perverted.
They are without arising and without activity;
they are neither conditioned nor abiding, yet not unconditioned.
It is not the domain of the mind; it is quiescent and signless.
For this reason, to see the twelve links of dependent origination is itself to see the Dharma.
Arising constantly in succession yet without birth;
seeing reality as it is, without inversion;
without birth and without action.
It is neither conditioned nor non-abiding unconditioned;
it is not the domain of the mind, being quiescent and signless.
For this reason:
To see the twelve links of dependent origination is to see the Dharma-body, which is fully endowed with the unsurpassed path.
The Venerable Śāriputra asked Maitreya:
"What is meant by 'twelve links of dependent origination'?
Maitreya replied,
"That which has causes and conditions is called the dharma of dependent origination."
This is the Buddha’s brief explanation of the characteristics of causes and conditions.
By means of these causes, this fruit is produced.
Such is the Dharma of dependent origination that arises through causes and conditions for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
The Tathāgata’s non-appearance in the world is likewise a dharma born of causes and conditions;
its nature and characteristics are eternally abiding and free from all afflictions.
It is ultimately suchness, not otherwise.
This is the true Dharma, the Dharma free from inversion.
Furthermore, the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination arises from two kinds.
What are these two?
First is the cause;
second is the fruit.
Furthermore, phenomena produced by causes and conditions are of two kinds.
There are internal conditions and there are external conditions.
From what do external conditioned phenomena arise?
Just as a seed is able to produce a sprout,
from the sprout a leaf arises,
and from the leaf a node arises.
From the joints the stalks grow;
from the stalks the ears grow;
from the ears the flowers grow.
From the flower, the fruit is produced;
because there is no seed, there is no sprout,
and so on, until there is neither flower nor fruit.
Because the seed exists, the sprout arises;
and so on, up to: because the flower exists, the fruit arises.
Yet the seed does not think, "I am able to produce the sprout."
The bud also does not form the thought, "I am produced from the seed. ...
And so on, up to: the flower also does not form the thought, "I am able to produce the fruit.
The fruit also does not form the thought, "I am produced from the flower."
In reality, it is the seed that is able to produce the sprout;
this is called an external phenomenon produced by causes.
What is called an external phenomenon produced by conditions?
These are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and time.
The element of earth is characterized by solidity;
the element of water is characterized by moisture.
The fire element matures;
the wind element initiates;
the space element does not create obstruction.
Furthermore, depending on the seasonal changes of time and harmony,
when these six conditions are fully present, [the thing] arises;
if the six conditions are not complete, the thing does not arise.
When the six conditions— earth, water, fire, wind, space, and time—
are in harmony, neither increasing nor decreasing,
things are then produced.
The earth does not say, "I am able to support.
Water does not say, "I am able to moisten.
Fire does not say, "I am able to ripen."
The wind also does not say, "I am able to initiate [it].
Space also does not say, "I am able to refrain from creating obstacles.
Time also does not say, "I am able to cause it to arise."
The seed does not say, "I have produced the sprout through these six conditions," nor does the sprout say,
"I have arisen from these various conditions.
Although they do not form such thoughts, [the sprout] arises from those various conditions.
In reality, the sprout arises from the combination of various conditions;
it does not arise from itself,
nor does it arise from another.
Nor does it arise from a combination of self and other;
nor does it arise from Īśvara, nor from time or space,
nor does it arise from primordial nature (prakṛti).
Nor does it arise without a cause;
this is called the sequence of the dharma of arising.
Thus, the external dependent origination of dharmas is established by way of five factors.
One should know that it is neither annihilated nor eternal, and it does not pass from here to there.
Just as a sprout is small while its fruit is manifold,
so too does a similar continuity arise without producing anything dissimilar.
What is meant by "not being annihilated"?
It is because it continues in succession through the sequence of seed, sprout, root, and stem that it is not annihilated.
What is meant by "not being eternal"?
Because the sprout, stem, flower, and fruit are each distinct from one another, they are impermanent.
Furthermore, the sprout does not arise after the seed has been extinguished,
nor does it arise without the seed having ceased.
Furthermore, because the sprout of the law of dependent origination arises as the seed perishes,
it is impermanent due to its sequential production;
and because the names and characteristics of the seed and the sprout are each distinct.
It does not go from here to there;
because the seed is small while the fruit is great, one should know that they are not identical.
This is called "the seed being small and the fruit being great."
Just as a seed does not produce a different fruit,
it is called a "similar continuity.
By means of these five kinds of external conditions, all phenomena are able to arise.
The internal law of dependent origination arises from two kinds [of causes].
What are these causes?
From ignorance up to old age and death.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;
thus, up to: with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease.
Because of ignorance, volitional formations exist.
...up to the point that because there is birth, there is aging and death.
Ignorance does not say, "I am able to produce volitional formations," nor do volitional formations say, "I am produced from ignorance."
Even up to old age, sickness, and death, they do not say, "I arise from birth.
Yet, in reality, when there is ignorance, there are volitional formations;
when there is birth, there is old age and death.
This is called the sequence of dharmas arising from internal causes.
What is called the dharma of dependent origination through internal conditions?
It refers to the six elements.
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
What is meant by "earth"?
That which is capable of firm support is called the earth element.
What is called water?
That which is capable of moistening and soaking is termed the water element (*abdhātu*).
What is called fire?
That which can mature is called the fire element.
What is wind? That which enables inhalation and exhalation is called the wind element.
What is meant by "space"?
That which is capable of being without obstruction is called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
What is meant by "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)?
The four aggregates and the five consciousnesses are called "name" (*nāma*) and are also called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
The conjunction of these various factors is called the "body" (*kāya*).
The mind associated with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*) is called "consciousness."
These four aggregates, together with the five sense organs, are called form (*rūpa*).
These six conditions collectively are called the body (*kāya*).
When these six conditions are complete and without deficiency, the body is thereby formed.
If these conditions were diminished, the body would not be formed;
the earth does not think, "I can provide firm support," nor does the water think, "I can provide moisture."
Fire does not think, "I am able to bring things to maturity.
Wind does not think, "I am able to produce inhalation and exhalation.
Space does not think, "I am able to provide non-obstruction."
Consciousness does not think, "I am able to produce and grow this body," nor does the body think, "I have arisen from various conditions.
If these six conditions were absent, the body would not arise either.
The earth element is also without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span; it is neither male nor female, nor is it neither male nor female; it is neither this nor that.
Water, fire, wind, and even consciousness and so forth are likewise all without self, without sentient being, and without life-span.
...up to and including being neither this nor that.
What is called ignorance?
Ignorance is as follows:
Within the six elements, one gives rise to the notion of unity,

the notion of a collection, the notion of permanence, the notion of immovability, the notion of indestructibility, and internally gives rise to the notion of pleasure, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, the notion of a person, the notion of a self, and the notion of "mine."
To give rise to such various and manifold perceptions is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
From within these five sense-faculties, craving and aversion arise.
The same applies to perception and mental formations.
That which follows along with all dharmas of provisional designation is called consciousness.
These four aggregates constitute "name."
The aggregate of form is "form";
this is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
From the growth of name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise.
The increase of the six sense bases gives rise to contact;
the increase of contact gives rise to feeling;
the increase of feeling gives rise to craving.
The increase of craving gives rise to grasping;
the increase of grasping gives rise to becoming.
Because becoming increases, it is able to produce the subsequent aggregates, which constitutes birth.
The growth and transformation of birth is called aging;
the decay and disintegration of the aggregate of sensation is called death;
and that which gives rise to envy and feverish distress is called sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
The five sense-faculties being afflicted by adverse conditions is called bodily suffering;
the mind being in a state of disharmony is called mental suffering.
The accumulation of such various sufferings, which constantly exists in darkness, is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
The accumulation of various karmas is called *saṃskāra* (formations).
The discernment of various phenomena is called *vijñāna* (consciousness).
That which establishes [a basis] is called *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form).
The unfolding of the six faculties is called the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Because they encounter conditions and grasp objects, it is called contact (*sparśa*).
Because one experiences and perceives suffering and pleasure, it is called feeling (*vedanā*).
Because it is like a thirst for drink, it is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
because it is able to grasp at objects, it is called grasping (*upādāna*);
and because it initiates the performance of various karmas, it is called becoming (*bhava*).
Because the subsequent aggregates first arise, it is called birth (*jāti*).
Because they abide in the world and undergo decay and change, it is called old age (*jarā*).
Because they finally perish and disintegrate, it is called death (*maraṇa*).
To feel regret for past events with a voice of sorrow and distress is called *daurmanasya* (sorrowful suffering).
For circumstances to come and press upon the person is called *duḥkha* (suffering/distress).
Because this recollection continues in succession, it is called *śoka* (lamentation/grief).
Being bound by the afflictions is called "distress" (*upāyāsa*).
Erroneous views and false understandings are called "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

Because these erroneous understandings give rise to the three types of karma, they are called "formative activities" (*saṃskāra*). Because these good and evil karmas are able to receive their retributive fruits, they are called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
From defiled and neutral karma arises defiled and neutral consciousness;
from immovable karma arises immovable consciousness;
from consciousness arise name-and-form.
From name-and-form arise the six sense bases;
from the six sense bases arises contact;
from contact arises feeling.
From sensation arises craving;
from craving arises grasping;
from grasping arises becoming.
From existence arises birth;
from birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
Maitreya spoke thus to the Venerable Śāriputra.
Each of the twelve links of dependent origination has its own fruit;
they are neither eternal nor annihilated,
neither conditioned nor separate from the conditioned.
It is not the dharma of exhaustion;
it is not the dharma of dispassion;
it is not the dharma of cessation.
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, this continuity remains uninterrupted,
like the swift current of a river that never ceases for even a moment.
At that time, Maitreya spoke again to the Venerable Śāriputra.
Each of the twelve links of dependent origination has its own cause and its own condition;
they are neither eternal nor annihilated.
It is not conditioned, yet it is not separate from the conditioned;
it is not a dharma of exhaustion,
nor is it a dharma of detachment.
It is not a phenomenon subject to extinction.
Whether a Buddha appears or does not appear, it continues in succession without interruption,
like the rapid flow of a river that never ceases for even a moment.
One can cause the twelve links of dependent origination to increase by means of four conditions. What are these four?
They are ignorance, craving, karma, and consciousness.
Consciousness constitutes the essence of the seed;
karma constitutes the essence of the field;
and ignorance and craving constitute the essence of the afflictions.
It is capable of producing consciousness;
karma serves as the field for consciousness,
and craving serves as the moisture that saturates it.
Ignorance covers and plants the seed of consciousness.
Karma does not think, "I am able to produce the seed of consciousness," nor does craving think, "I am able to moisten it."
Ignorance also does not form the thought, "I am able to cover and plant the seed of consciousness.
Consciousness likewise does not form the thought, "I [arise] from such causes and conditions.
Furthermore, karma serves as the field for consciousness.
Ignorance serves as the filth,
and the water of craving serves as the moisture;
thus, the sprouts of name-and-form and so forth are produced.
Furthermore, the sprout of name-and-form does not arise from itself,
nor does it arise from another,
nor does it arise from a combination of both self and other.
Nor is it born from Īśvara;
nor is it born from time or space;
nor is it born from a primal substance; nor is it born without causes and conditions.
Furthermore, the sprout of form arises from the conjunction of various conditions, such as desire, pleasure, paternal seed, and maternal blood;
it is without a master, without a self, without a creator, and without a life-principle.
It is like space and like an illusion.
It arises from the combination of various causes and conditions.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra,
visual consciousness arises from five causal conditions.
What are the five?
When there is the eye, visible forms, light, space,
and attention, consciousness arises.
Visual consciousness relies upon the eye-faculty and takes visible form as its object;
it depends upon light for illumination and does not encounter obstruction from empty space,
because it is activated by mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Visual consciousness arises.
Thus, if these various conditions do not come together, visual consciousness does not arise;
yet visual consciousness itself does not form the thought, "I am able to produce the perception of a body."
Form does not form the thought, "I am able to act as an object.
Clarity does not form the thought, "I am able to illuminate and perceive.
Space does not form the thought, "I am able to be unobstructed."
The mental attention (*manasikāra*) does not form the thought,
"I am able to initiate visual consciousness," nor does the visual consciousness form the thought, "I have arisen from various conditions.
In this way, visual consciousness is truly conventional (*prajñapti*).
It arises from the conjunction of various conditions.
In this same sequence, the sense faculties give rise to consciousness;
it is explained in this manner.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there is no dharma that passes from this world to another world; rather,
it is simply through the conjunction of various conditions adorned by karma and its fruits that [a being] arises.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
it is like a bright mirror that can manifest the image of a face;
yet the mirror and the face each exist in different locations.
Yet there is no coming or going, and objects appear as being in the same place.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
it is like the moon beautifying the sky, forty-two thousand yojanas from the earth.
The flowing water is below while the moon is above;
although the celestial phenomenon is one, its reflection appears in the many waters.
The substance of the moon does not descend, nor does the quality of the water ascend.
In this way, Śāriputra,
sentient beings do not go from this world to a future world,
nor do they return from a future world back to this one.
Nevertheless, the karmic fruits, causes, conditions,
and retributions cannot be diminished.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra:
Just as fire, having obtained fuel, burns until the fuel is exhausted and then ceases,
so too does the consciousness that links rebirth through the fetters of karma pervade all realms of existence and is able to give rise to the fruit of name-and-form.
It is without self, without master, and without recipient;
it is like space,
like a mirage in the heat.
Like an illusion or a dream, there are no real dharmas;
yet the karmic causes and conditions of good and evil, along with their retributions, do not perish according to one's actions.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra:
The twelve links of dependent origination also arise from five conditions:
they are neither eternal nor annihilated; they do not come or go; a small cause produces a great fruit;
and they arise in a sequential succession of similar continuity.
What is impermanence?
One aggregate ceases and another aggregate arises;
that which ceases is not itself that which arises, and that which arises is not itself that which ceases.
Therefore, it is called "impermanent.
Why is it not "interrupted"?
It is like the rising and falling of a scale: as this ceases, that arises.
Therefore, it is called "uninterrupted.
To know and see it as it truly is:
how is it that there is no coming or going, and yet, without a seed departing, it arrives at the sprout?
Nor does the sprout come from anywhere to reach the location of the seed;
for this reason,
there is no movement from here to there.
However, in reality, a small seed can produce many fruits;
how then could they arise as something dissimilar?
For example, an unwholesome cause produces an unwholesome fruit.
Just as a virtuous cause gives rise to a virtuous fruit,
for this reason it is called arising through a similar succession.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:
As the Buddha has taught:
"To be able to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination is called right view."
If one correctly contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination,
one does not give rise to the notion of existence regarding the body of the past,
nor does one give rise to the notion of non-existence regarding the body of the future.
From where do sentient beings come, and to where do they go?
Whether they be śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or people of the world, they are possessed of various views:
the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-principle, the view of a person, and views regarding what is auspicious and inauspicious.
In this way, the twelve links of dependent origination are like a tāla tree whose head has been cut off; it can never grow again,
and thus my [wrong] views are eliminated.
If a person correctly perceives the twelve links of dependent origination and attains such a mind of reflection,
Venerable Śāriputra.
If there are sentient beings who can endure this Dharma,
[they shall see] this Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Charioteer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
He will certainly be granted the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having heard these words spoken by Maitreya, the Venerable Śāriputra departed with joy.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and the great assembly prostrated themselves before Maitreya and joyfully practiced his teachings.
The Sūtra on the Rice Seedling Spoken by the Buddha
